label: question:eremenko
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{question:eremenko}
On any compact Riemann surface, the set of Fuchsian equations with prescribed singularities and exponents, and with unitarizable monodromy is finite.
head: environment
name: Eremenko

label: thm:unitary
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitary}
Let $X$ be a compact connected Riemann surface, let $D=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\subset X$ be a finite set of distinct points, and let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n\in\mathbb R$. There are only finitely many meromorphic projective connections that are holomorphic outside $D$, have poles of order at most two along $D$, have coefficients $(1-\beta_i^2)/4$ of the $z^{-2}$ terms at $a_i$, and have unitarizable projective monodromy.

label: def:unitarizable-projective-monodromy
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:unitarizable-projective-monodromy}
Let $\rho_Q^{\mathrm{proj}}:\Gamma\to\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be the projectivization of $\rho_Q$. The equation has \emph{unitarizable projective monodromy} if there is $M\in\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ such that
\[
 M\rho_Q^{\mathrm{proj}}(\Gamma)M^{-1}\subset\operatorname{PSU}(2).
\]

label: lem:growth
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\mu=\sqrt{1+\lVert Q-Q_0\rVert}$. Along fixed representative paths covered by finitely many compact coordinate sets, $|Q_z|\le C\mu^2$. For the row solution matrix $Y_z$ with rows $(y_i,y_i')$, set $D_\mu=\operatorname{diag}(\mu^{1/2},\mu^{-1/2})$. Then
\[
 (Y_zD_\mu)'=(Y_zD_\mu)\begin{pmatrix}0&-Q_z/\mu\\ \mu&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Along these paths, the norm of this coefficient is at most $C\mu$ times the path speed. At a coordinate change, the balanced row matrix changes by $D_\mu^{-1}G^{\mathsf t}D_\mu$, with $G$ as in \eqref{eq:jet-transition}. Its diagonal entries are fixed and bounded away from zero; its off-diagonal entry is a fixed bounded function divided by $\mu$. Both this matrix and its inverse are bounded on the chosen overlaps. By Gronwall's inequality and the finiteness of the coordinate transitions, the norms of the transfer matrices and their inverses are bounded by $\exp(C_\eta\mu)$.

The transfer around a based loop is conjugate to its monodromy. Since its spectral radius is at most its norm, we obtain \eqref{eq:word-growth}. If $A$ is the balanced frame at the common initial point and $P_\eta$ is the loop transfer, then $\rho_Q(\eta)A=AP_\eta$. The displacement of $AA^*$ is $2\log\lVert P_\eta\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$. Using the same initial frame for all generators proves the last assertion.

title: Proposition

title: Proof

label: def:tree-length
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:tree-length}
An $\mathbb R$-tree is a metric space in which any two points are joined by a unique arc and that arc is isometric to a real interval. For an isometry $h$ of a metric space $(M,d)$, its translation length is $\inf_{x\in M}d(x,hx)$. We write $\ell_T(h)$ for this length in a tree $T$. For a marked group action, we call $\eta\mapsto\ell_T(\eta)$ the \emph{marked length function}.
head: environment
name: Real trees and translation lengths

label: prop:tree-map
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $q_j\to q\ne0$ in $V$, the quantity $\sqrt{1+\lVert Q_j-Q_0\rVert}$ is comparable with $\lambda_j$. At each fixed regular point, the diagonal matrices in \eqref{eq:hyperbolic-frame} are uniformly comparable to those used for the coarse balancing in Lemma~\ref{lem:growth}. Finite representative paths therefore give $O(\lambda_j)$ based displacements for every generator, and for every fixed word. It follows that the monodromy actions induce an action on the pointed ultralimit \eqref{eq:cone}.

For a regular lifted point $z$, continue the fundamental solutions along a fixed path and take the ultralimit of $H_j(z)$. The same coarse estimate bounds its rescaled distance from the basepoint. The coordinate discrepancy \eqref{eq:coordinate-distance} vanishes after rescaling, so the point is independent of the coordinate chart. The theta cocycle and analytic continuation ensure compatibility along chart chains and equivariance. By Proposition~\ref{prop:local-limit}, two points of a regular rectangle have limiting distance $|u(z)-u(w)|$. Points at equal heights have the same image, while distinct heights determine an isometric interval, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:local-height}. This proves \eqref{eq:height-model} and nonconstancy.

Subdivision of any regular piecewise smooth path gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flat-path}
 d_T(f(x),f(y))\le\int_{x}^{y}|q|^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
Near a point where $q=z^kh(z)\,dz^2$, $h(0)\ne0$, with $k\ge-1$, radial tails and circular arcs of bounded angle have flat length $O(r^{1+k/2})$. At an ordinary zero, completeness of $T$ then gives a unique continuous extension. At a marked simple pole they give a radial endpoint and an $O(\sqrt r)$ bound in a fundamental angular sector. A full peripheral turn has length tending to zero, so equivariance makes the peripheral element fix that endpoint. Since its powers also fix the endpoint, the same bound holds in every lifted angular sector. At a mark where the simple pole cancels, the corresponding holomorphic estimate is stronger.
head: environment

label: lem:displacement
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a hyperbolic tree isometry the two displacements are $2r+2\ell_T(h)$ and $2r+\ell_T(h)$, where $r$ is distance to its axis. For an elliptic isometry, displacement is twice the distance to its fixed subtree and $\operatorname{Fix}(h)\subset\operatorname{Fix}(h^2)$. The standard formulas for tree isometries \cite[Section~1.3]{CM87} therefore give \eqref{eq:tree-displacement}.

In $\mathbb H^3$, suppose first that $h$ is loxodromic or nonidentity elliptic, with axis distance $r$ and rotation angle $\theta$. Set $L=L(h)$ and $A_\nu=\sinh(d_\nu/2)$. Cylindrical coordinates give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cylindrical}
 A_\nu^2=\sinh^2(\nu L/2)\cosh^2r+\sin^2(\nu\theta/2)\sinh^2r.
\end{equation}
Thus $A_2\le2\cosh(L/2)A_1$, and $\operatorname{arsinh}(kx)-\operatorname{arsinh} x\le\log k$ for $k\ge1$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:displacement-upper}
 d_2-d_1\le2\log(2\cosh(L/2))\le L+2\log2.
\end{equation}
For $L\ge1$ we also have
\[
 A_1\le\cosh(L/2)\cosh r,\quad
 A_2\ge2\sinh(L/2)A_1,\quad A_1\ge\sinh(1/2)>1/2.
\]
Using $\operatorname{arsinh}(kx)\ge\log(2kx)$ and $\operatorname{arsinh} x\le\log(2x)+\log((1+\sqrt5)/2)$ for $x\ge1/2$, we obtain
\[
 d_2-d_1\ge L+2\log(1-e^{-L})-2\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}>L-4.
\]
When $L<1$, the lower bound follows from the nonnegativity of the maximum. In the parabolic case $L=0$ and $A_2=2A_1$, which gives the same upper bound; the identity is immediate. This proves \eqref{eq:hyperbolic-displacement}.
head: environment

label: lem:nonzero-length
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:nonzero-length}
The action on $T$ has a nonzero marked length function.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If all lengths vanish, all group elements are elliptic. The fixed subtrees of two generators intersect, since otherwise their product has positive length. By the finite Helly property for subtrees, the generators have a common fixed point $a$; see \cite[Sections~1.2--1.5]{CM87}.

The function $d_T(f,a)^2$ descends to $X^\circ$. On a regular rectangle it is a convex function of the real harmonic coordinate in \eqref{eq:height-model}, hence subharmonic. A continuous convex function of finitely many harmonic functions is subharmonic: this follows by the chain rule for a smooth convex function and by local convolution in general. The endpoint bounds allow us to extend the function subharmonically across every omitted point. By the maximum principle on the compact connected curve, the resulting function is constant \cite[Chapters~2--3]{Ran95}. Distance to a fixed point in a tree cannot be constant on a nondegenerate interval, contradicting the local form of $f$.
head: environment

label: prop:properness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:properness}
For arbitrary fixed complex coefficients $\boldsymbol\delta$, the maps $F_X$ and $\operatorname{Hol}_X$ are proper.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
An escaping sequence with bounded finite traces has bounded traces for every fixed word by \eqref{eq:trace-identities}. The eigenvalues of its monodromy matrices, and hence their translation lengths, are bounded word by word. Normalize the sequence as in \eqref{eq:normalized}. Equation~\eqref{eq:length-limit} makes every length in the limiting tree zero, contrary to Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero-length}. Thus the inverse image under $F_X$ of a compact set is bounded. It is closed by continuity, hence compact in $\mathcal A_X\simeq\mathbb C^m$.

For compact $C\subset\mathcal X(\Gamma)$, the closed set $\operatorname{Hol}_X^{-1}(C)$ is contained in the compact set $F_X^{-1}(\tau(C))$. Hence the holonomy map is proper as well.
head: environment

label: cor:finite-holonomy
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:finite-holonomy}
Every complex character has finitely many realizations in $\mathcal A_X$. With its reduced analytic structure, the image $\mathcal Y_X=\operatorname{Hol}_X(\mathcal A_X)$ is closed, irreducible, and of dimension $m$, and $\operatorname{Hol}_X:\mathcal A_X\to\mathcal Y_X$ is finite holomorphic. The same conclusions hold for the trace map onto its image.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Each fiber is a compact analytic subset of an affine complex space and is therefore finite. Indeed, on any hypothetical positive-dimensional component the strictly plurisubharmonic function $\lVert z\rVert^2$ attains a maximum, contradicting the maximum principle on a local nonconstant analytic curve through that point \cite{Chi89}. A proper holomorphic map with finite fibers is finite, and its image is analytic by Remmert's theorem \cite[Chapter~I, Section~2]{Fre16}. The image is irreducible because the source is irreducible, and it has dimension $m$ by the dimension theorem for finite maps.
head: environment

label: prop:trace-growth
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $C\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb C)$ choose an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of modulus at least one. Then
\[
 |\operatorname{tr} C|\le2e^{L(C)/2},\quad |\lambda|\le|\operatorname{tr} C|+1.
\]
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:growth} to the finitely many coordinate words gives the upper bound everywhere. If the lower bound fails, choose $Q_j$ with $T_j=\lVert Q_j-Q_0\rVert\to\infty$ and $\Lambda_X(Q_j)/\sqrt{T_j}\to0$, and extract a nonzero normalized limit $q$. Since each word trace is a fixed polynomial in the finite traces,
\[
 \log\bigl(2+|\operatorname{tr}\rho_{Q_j}(\eta)|\bigr)\le C_\eta\bigl(1+\Lambda_X(Q_j)\bigr).
\]
By the eigenvalue bound, every normalized word length tends to zero. This contradicts \eqref{eq:length-limit} and Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero-length}. We obtain \eqref{eq:accessory-trace-bound} by squaring the lower estimate and increasing the constant on a compact ball.
head: environment

label: prop:relative-properness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:relative-properness}
In the setting \eqref{eq:relative-accessory}, the relative maps
\[
 (b,Q)\longmapsto(b,\operatorname{Hol}_{X_b}(Q)),\quad
 (b,Q)\longmapsto(b,F_{X_b}(Q))
\]
are holomorphic and proper. For each compact $K\Subset B$ and $m>0$, there are $c_K,C_K,R_K>0$ such that, for $b\in K$ and $T=\lVert Q-Q_0(b)\rVert\ge R_K$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-growth}
 c_K\sqrt T\le\log\left(2+\max_{w\in\mathcal W}|\operatorname{tr}\rho_Q(w)|\right)
 \le C_K\sqrt{1+T}.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin with the geometric construction needed for uniformity. A proper smooth submersion with disjoint sections admits a local smooth trivialization that preserves the sections. To construct such a trivialization, we choose horizontal lifts of coordinate fields on the base and add vertical corrections so that the lifts agree with the derivatives of the sections. Since the section images have disjoint neighborhoods, we can choose these corrections independently. Over a smaller coordinate ball, the time-one flow of the lift of the radial field from its center stays over a compact base set; properness gives existence of the flow and its inverse. The resulting diffeomorphisms preserve each section and depend smoothly on the base parameter. We can therefore transport fixed topological paths through finitely many relatively compact relative charts, with uniformly bounded $C^1$ coordinate parametrizations.

Suppose $b_j\to b_0$ and $Q_j=Q_0(b_j)+T_jq_j$, where $T_j=\lVert Q_j-Q_0(b_j)\rVert\to\infty$. After passing to a subsequence, the normalized coefficient vectors converge. In the holomorphic frame of $V_b$, their limit defines $q\ne0$ on $X_{b_0}$. On compact relative coordinate disks, the coefficients of $q_j$ and all their fiber derivatives converge to those of $q$, by holomorphicity and Cauchy's estimates. At a marked section $z=0$, the functions $zq_{j,z}$ are holomorphic and converge in the same manner, so $q$ has at most simple poles.

Along the transported compact paths, the coefficients of $Q_0(b_j)$, the transition functions, and their derivatives are uniformly bounded; the coordinate derivatives are also bounded away from zero. With $\lambda_j=\sqrt{T_j}$, the coarse balanced transition has the form
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}t^{-1/2}&-t_w/(2\lambda_j t^{3/2})\\0&t^{1/2}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both this matrix and its inverse have uniformly bounded norms. Gronwall therefore gives uniform $O(\lambda_j)$ generator displacements. On any compact regular disk of the limit differential, the roots $\sqrt{q_j}$, their natural coordinates, and their inverse coordinate derivatives converge uniformly with the required derivatives. The functions $W_j$ in \eqref{eq:liouville} are uniformly bounded there. Consequently, the constants in \eqref{eq:shear-distance}--\eqref{eq:singular-value} can be chosen uniformly along this moving sequence. This proves the local height limit for transported points on the limiting curve, with the exact scale $1/(2\lambda_j)$.

We form a single pointed ultralimit and use the transported points to define a map from the punctured universal cover of $X_{b_0}$. The transition estimates ensure that these definitions agree on overlaps, while the marking gives equivariance. Its local image is the isometric height interval of $q$. Inequality~\eqref{eq:flat-path} now holds in this limit tree. The radial and angular estimates for the limit differential extend the map across its zeros and give peripheral endpoints, uniformly over all angular sectors after using the peripheral isometry. These estimates apply to the map in the limiting tree. The compact-surface maximum argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero-length}, on $X_{b_0}$, proves nonzero length. In fact, some word in the finite set $\mathcal W$ has positive length: if all these lengths vanished, the generators would be elliptic with pairwise intersecting fixed subtrees, and Helly's property would give a common fixed point. Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:displacement} gives the exact wordwise length comparison in the moving family.

Monodromy is jointly holomorphic in $(b,Q)$. To verify this, we follow each marked loop through finitely many relative disks, use holomorphic point sections on overlaps to continue the initial-value solution, and apply the locally uniformly convergent Picard series to the coefficient and jet transition matrices. Local changes of representatives only conjugate monodromy. Hence traces and characters are holomorphic on the whole chart.

Suppose a sequence remains over a compact subset of the base and character space, but its coefficients are unbounded. After passing to a subsequence, we can apply the preceding construction. Each word in $\mathcal W$ has bounded trace, so \eqref{eq:length-limit} gives zero length on $\mathcal W$, a contradiction. The same reasoning applies directly to bounded finite traces. Hence the coefficients are bounded over compact target sets locally. Finite-dimensional compactness and continuity give properness of both relative maps. Rank zero is immediate from the affine origin.

To prove the lower estimate in \eqref{eq:relative-growth}, suppose that a sequence $b_j\in K$, $T_j\to\infty$, satisfies
\[
 \max_{w\in\mathcal W}\frac{L(\rho_{Q_j}(w))}{2\sqrt{T_j}}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Compactness of $K$ and the normalized coefficient sphere gives the limit construction above, contradicting its positive length on $\mathcal W$. We therefore obtain a uniform positive lower bound beyond a fixed threshold. If $w$ realizes this lower bound, then
\[
 |\operatorname{tr}\rho_Q(w)|\ge e^{c\sqrt T}-e^{-c\sqrt T}.
\]
After increasing the threshold if necessary, we obtain the lower logarithmic estimate. The upper estimate follows from the uniform compact-path Gronwall bounds and $|\operatorname{tr} C|\le2e^{L(C)/2}$.
head: environment

label: def:abelian-length
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:abelian-length}
A marked length function of an action of $\Gamma$ on an $\mathbb R$-tree is \emph{abelian} if it has the form $\eta\mapsto|c(\eta)|$ for a homomorphism $c:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$. Otherwise it is \emph{nonabelian}. We follow the terminology of Culler--Morgan for semisimple actions. In particular, actions preserving a line, including those with reflections, are semisimple \cite{CM87}.
head: environment
name: Abelian length functions

label: lem:minimal-tree
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:minimal-tree}
The action on $T$ has a unique minimal invariant subtree $T_{\min}$, and $f$ takes values in its completion $T_c$, realized as its closure in $T$. Two such actions with the same nonabelian marked length function have equivariantly isometric completed minimal subtrees.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The existence and uniqueness of $T_{\min}$ follow from the nonzero length function and \cite[Proposition~3.1]{CM87}. Its closure $T_c$ in the complete tree is closed, convex, and invariant. The function $d_T(f,T_c)^2$ descends to $X^\circ$. On a regular rectangle, it is a convex function of the harmonic height $u=\operatorname{Im}\int\sqrt q$, hence is subharmonic. The endpoint estimates in Proposition~\ref{prop:tree-map} give boundedness at the punctures and zeros. Removability and the maximum principle make it constant on $X$ \cite[Chapters~2--3]{Ran95}. A level set of positive distance from a convex subtree contains no nondegenerate interval: along a segment outside the subtree the distance has slope $1$ or $-1$, apart from a possible minimum. Since $f$ has a nondegenerate local interval as image, the constant is zero. Hence $f$ takes values in $T_c$.

A nonsemisimple action has an abelian length function by \cite[Corollary~2.4]{CM87}. The actions in the last assertion are therefore semisimple. On their minimal subtrees, \cite[Theorem~3.7]{CM87} gives an equivariant isometry. It extends uniquely to metric completions, which proves the assertion.
head: environment

label: prop:constant-distance
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:constant-distance}
Let $f_1,f_2:\widetilde{X^\circ}\to T$ be nonconstant maps equivariant for the same action of $\Gamma$ on a complete $\mathbb R$-tree. Suppose that outside the lifts of a finite set they have the form $f_1=\iota\circ u$ and $f_2=\jmath\circ v$, where $u,v$ are real harmonic coordinates with nonzero differential and $\iota,\jmath$ are isometric interval embeddings. Suppose also that the descended function $d_T(f_1,f_2)^2$ is bounded near every puncture and exceptional point. Then this function is constant, and $(\partial u)^2=(\partial v)^2$ on each common regular disk.
head: environment

label: eq:convex-distance
title: Proof
head: environment

label: prop:abelian-reconstruction
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:busemann-period
title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Corollary~2.3]{CM87}, an action with a nonzero abelian length function fixes an end. Choose the Busemann function \eqref{eq:busemann} for that end. Invariance of the end gives a homomorphism $c:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:busemann-period}
 b_T(\eta x)=b_T(x)+c(\eta).
\end{equation}
We verify the normalization directly. The rays $r$ and $\eta r$ have a common tail, on which $\eta r(t)=r(t+s_\eta)$ for a constant $s_\eta$. Thus $c(\eta)=-s_\eta$. At a point sufficiently far along that ray, the displacements under $\eta$ and $\eta^2$ are $|s_\eta|$ and $2|s_\eta|$. The tree identity in Lemma~\ref{lem:displacement} gives $\ell_T(\eta)=|s_\eta|=|c(\eta)|$.

Set $h=b_T\circ f$. On a regular disk this is a convex function of the real harmonic height, so it is subharmonic. The local branches differ by the constants in \eqref{eq:busemann-period}. At an ordinary zero of $q$, continuity of $f$ makes the local branch bounded and continuously extendible. At a marked point, let $P_i$ be the endpoint fixed by the peripheral element $\gamma_i$. Then
\[
 c(\gamma_i)=b_T(\gamma_i P_i)-b_T(P_i)=0.
\]
Consequently $h$ has a single-valued branch on the punctured disk. The endpoint bound makes this branch bounded, and it extends subharmonically and continuously over the puncture. We have thus extended the local branches across the omitted points before taking their differentials.

On each connected component of an overlap, any two branches differ by a constant. Their distributional differentials therefore define a global real one-form $\alpha=dh$ in the sense of currents. Choose a smooth conformal metric on $X$ and let $*$ be its Hodge star on real one-forms, with $*dx=dy$ and $*dy=-dx$ in an oriented isothermal coordinate. The current
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positive-current}
 \mu=d(*\alpha)
\end{equation}
is locally the distributional Laplacian of a subharmonic branch times area, hence is a nonnegative measure on $X$. Moreover, this measure is the exterior derivative of a global current. Pairing with the constant function $1$ gives
\[
 \mu(X)=\int_X d(*\alpha)=0.
\]
Thus $\mu=0$. By regularity for distributional harmonic functions, every branch of $h$ is smooth and harmonic. It follows that $\alpha$ is a smooth closed and co-closed real one-form on the compact curve. We use here the standard regularity and Hodge-theoretic facts for harmonic differentials \cite{For81,Ran95}.

On a regular disk write $f=\iota(u)$, where $u=\operatorname{Im}\int\sqrt q$. The restriction of $b_T$ to $\iota(u)$ is affine with slope $1$ or $-1$, except possibly for one convex corner. Since $du\ne0$, a corner inside the height range would make $b_T\circ\iota\circ u$ nonsmooth there, or equivalently would give it a positive distributional Laplacian supported on a level curve. Since the potential is harmonic, no such corner can occur. Hence $dh=du$ or $dh=-du$ locally. As
\[
 (u_z)^2\,dz^2=-\tfrac14q,
\]
we obtain \eqref{eq:abelian-square} on every regular disk. The $(1,0)$ part of a real harmonic form is holomorphic. By meromorphic continuation, \eqref{eq:abelian-square} holds on all of $X$; in particular, any possible simple pole of $q$ disappears.

The periods of $\alpha$ are exactly $c$. A real harmonic one-form on a compact curve is uniquely determined by its periods: the difference of two such forms is $dH$ for a global function $H$, and co-closedness makes $H$ harmonic, hence constant. Finally, if $c'$ is another homomorphism with $|c'|=|c|$, choose $\eta_0$ with $c(\eta_0)\ne0$ and put $c'(\eta_0)=\varepsilon c(\eta_0)$, where $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$. Equality of the squared values on $\eta_0$, $\eta$, and $\eta_0\eta$ gives
\[
 c(\eta_0)c(\eta)=c'(\eta_0)c'(\eta).
\]
Thus $c'=\varepsilon c$ on all of $\Gamma$. The corresponding harmonic form changes by the same global sign, which disappears upon squaring in \eqref{eq:abelian-square}. This proves uniqueness of $q$.
head: environment

label: prop:conjugate-limit
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $q\ne0$ and $p=0$. The accessory norm of the second sequence is $o(T_j)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:growth} then gives $L(\rho_{R_j}(\eta))=o(\sqrt{T_j})$ for every fixed word $\eta$. Equality of monodromy lengths and \eqref{eq:length-limit} would make the action associated with $q$ have zero length function, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero-length}. Interchanging the two sequences gives the same contradiction, so both limits are nonzero.

We use the common scale $1/(2\sqrt{T_j})$ and the same ultrafilter in both constructions. Equal finite traces give equal traces of all words, and hence equal hyperbolic translation lengths. By \eqref{eq:length-limit}, the two limiting actions have exactly equal nonzero marked length functions. If this function is abelian, Proposition~\ref{prop:abelian-reconstruction} and the conjugation of harmonic representatives just explained give \eqref{eq:conjugate-differential}.

If the common length function is nonabelian, Lemma~\ref{lem:minimal-tree} identifies the completed minimal trees equivariantly and places both maps in that common target. They have isometric interval descriptions on regular disks. The endpoint bounds ensure that the invariant squared distance is bounded at all marked points and zeros of either limiting differential. Real harmonic functions on $X$ and $\overline X$ are harmonic for the same underlying conformal metric, so Proposition~\ref{prop:constant-distance} applies.

To make the local comparison explicit, in a coordinate $z$ on $X$ write $q=q(z)\,dz^2$ and $p=P(w)\,dw^2$ on $\overline X$, where $w=\overline z$. The two local heights satisfy
\[
 u=\operatorname{Im}\int\sqrt q,\quad
 (u_z)^2\,dz^2=-\tfrac14q.
\]
If $v=\operatorname{Im}F(\overline z)$ with $F'(w)=\sqrt{P(w)}$, then
\[
 (v_z)^2\,dz^2=-\tfrac14\overline p.
\]
Equality of the squared derivatives gives \eqref{eq:conjugate-differential} on a common regular disk. The identity principle then extends it over $X$. When both structures are the same, both derivative formulas use that complex structure and give $p=q$.
head: environment

label: lem:psh
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:psh}
Let $A\subset\mathbb C^d$ be a closed complex analytic set. Suppose every limit of normalized points $x_j/\lVert x_j\rVert$, where $x_j\in A$ and $\lVert x_j\rVert\to\infty$, lies in a fixed totally real linear subspace of real dimension $d$. Then $A$ is discrete.
head: environment

label: eq:real-directions
title: Proof
body_md:
A complex-linear change of coordinates sends the given real subspace to $\mathbb R^d$. In the resulting coordinates the hypothesis implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:real-directions}
 \frac{|\operatorname{Im}\xi|}{|\xi|}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{as }|\xi|\to\infty,\quad \xi\in A.
\end{equation}
Otherwise, a sequence violating this limit would have a convergent normalized subsequence with a nonreal limit.

Fix $0<\varepsilon<1$ and put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:psh-function}
 B(\xi)=|\operatorname{Im}\xi|^2-\varepsilon|\operatorname{Re}\xi|^2.
\end{equation}
Its Levi matrix is $(1-\varepsilon)I_d/2$, so $B$ is strictly plurisubharmonic. Since $B=(1+\varepsilon)|\operatorname{Im}\xi|^2-\varepsilon|\xi|^2$, equation~\eqref{eq:real-directions} gives $B(\xi)\le-\varepsilon|\xi|^2/2$ on $A$ outside a large ball.

Suppose $C$ is a positive-dimensional irreducible component of $A$. The component is closed. For any $x\in C$, its nonempty superlevel set $\{y\in C:B(y)\ge B(x)\}$ is compact, so $B|_C$ has a maximum at some $x_*$. A positive-dimensional analytic germ contains a nonconstant holomorphic curve germ through its basepoint: take a one-dimensional analytic section and normalize a branch \cite{Chi89}. Thus there is a nonconstant holomorphic disk $h$ in $C$ with $h(0)=x_*$. The subharmonic function $B\circ h$ has an interior maximum and is constant. But
\[
 \frac{\partial^2(B\circ h)}{\partial t\,\partial\overline t}
 =\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2}\sum_{\nu=1}^d|h_\nu'(t)|^2,
\]
which would force $h$ to be constant. We conclude that no positive-dimensional components exist. A zero-dimensional analytic set is locally discrete \cite{Chi89}.

label: def:trace-relation
title: Definition
head: environment
name: The trace relation

label: prop:discrete-relation
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:discrete-relation}
The sets $\widetilde Z$ and $Z$ are closed and discrete.
head: environment

label: eq:real-subspace
title: Proof
body_md:
The case $m=0$ is immediate. Otherwise, let $(Q_j,R_j)\in\widetilde Z$ escape every compact subset and set
\[
 T_j=\max\{1,\lVert Q_j-Q_0\rVert,\lVert R_j-\overline{Q_0}\rVert\}.
\]
A subsequence of the normalized differences converges to $(q,p)$ with $\max\{\lVert q\rVert,\lVert p\rVert\}=1$. Proposition~\ref{prop:conjugate-limit} gives $p=\overline q$. The conclusion holds for every convergent normalized subsequence. Thus all directions at infinity lie in the totally real subspace
\begin{equation}\label{eq:real-subspace}
 L_{\mathbb R}=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^m:b=\overline a\}.
\end{equation}
The complex-linear coordinates
\[
 z=\frac{a+b}{2},\quad w=\frac{a-b}{2i}
\]
send $L_{\mathbb R}$ to $\mathbb R^{2m}$. By equivalence of norms, the normalization by $T_j$ is equivalent to Euclidean normalization. We can therefore apply Lemma~\ref{lem:psh} to $\widetilde Z$. Its closed analytic subset $Z$ is also discrete.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:properness}, the holonomy map is proper, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:discrete-relation}, $Z$ is discrete. To prove the final assertion, we consider the larger preimage under the finite-trace map
\[
 E^{\mathrm{tr}}=F_X^{-1}(K^{\mathrm{tr}}).
\]
This set is compact by properness. Every coordinate of $K^{\mathrm{tr}}$ is real, and coefficient conjugation satisfies \eqref{eq:conjugate-traces}. Hence
\[
 \{(Q,\overline Q):Q\in E^{\mathrm{tr}}\}\subset\widetilde Z.
\]
The graph on the left is compact and the set on the right is closed discrete, so the graph is finite. Projecting to the first factor identifies this graph with $E^{\mathrm{tr}}$. Finally $\operatorname{Hol}_X^{-1}(\mathcal K)\subset E^{\mathrm{tr}}$, which proves the theorem.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If the accessory space is empty, the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise, put $\delta_i=(1-\beta_i^2)/4$ and use the scalar lift defined by a theta characteristic. For a connection with unitarizable projective monodromy, we lift a projective conjugating element to $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb C)$. Each conjugated monodromy matrix belongs to the inverse image of $\operatorname{PSU}(2)$ under $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb C)\to\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The inverse image is $\operatorname{SU}(2)$: a determinant-one matrix projectively equal to $U\in\operatorname{SU}(2)$ is $cU$ with $c^2=1$. Its character lies in $\mathcal K$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:holonomy} gives finiteness.
head: environment

label: cor:image-intersection
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:image-intersection}
The intersection $\mathcal Y_X\cap\mathcal Y_{\overline X}$ is a closed discrete analytic subset of $\mathcal X(\Gamma)$. Every compact subset of $\mathcal X(\Gamma)$ contains only finitely many common characters and has only finitely many pairs in $Z$ above it.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a compact $K\subset\mathcal X(\Gamma)$, the pairs with common character in $K$ form the closed set
\[
 Z_K=Z\cap\bigl(\operatorname{Hol}_X^{-1}(K)\times\operatorname{Hol}_{\overline X}^{-1}(K)\bigr).
\]
By properness, this set is compact; by Proposition~\ref{prop:discrete-relation}, it is finite. The image of this set is exactly $K\cap\mathcal Y_X\cap\mathcal Y_{\overline X}$. Both holonomy images are closed analytic. Their intersection is therefore closed analytic. Since it meets each compact neighborhood in only finitely many points, it is discrete.
head: environment

label: rem:real-traces
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:real-traces}
The set of connections with real traces need not be finite. For a rectangular torus $\mathbb C/(a\mathbb Z+ib\mathbb Z)$, with $a,b>0$, let $z$ be its degree-two map to the sphere and write $dw/dz=1/\sqrt{P(z)}$ in an affine coordinate, where $P$ has the three finite branch values as simple roots. The developing maps $f_k(w)=\exp(2\pi k w/b)$ give sphere connections
\[
 Q_k(z)=-\frac{(2\pi k/b)^2}{4P(z)}+\frac12\mathcal S(w)(z),\quad k=1,2,\ldots.
\]
All four exponent differences are $1/2$. The torus periods act by a positive dilation and the identity, while the sheet involution acts by $f\mapsto1/f$. Conjugation by $f\mapsto if$ changes inversion to $f\mapsto-1/f$, so the projective monodromy lies in $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)$ and all scalar traces are real. The connections are distinct and unbounded. Thus discreteness of the real-trace set alone does not imply finiteness of the compact unitary locus.
head: environment
name: Real traces

label: rem:resonance
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:resonance}
At an integral exponent difference, the logarithmic Frobenius term and local Jordan form can vary within the accessory space. The estimates above are made along fixed paths outside $D$, while the bounds near punctures concern the limiting quadratic differential with at most simple poles. The preimage of the compact character set may contain connections with nonsemisimple monodromy. For example, on an unmarked torus the connection $Q=0$ with the trivial theta characteristic has unipotent monodromy and trivial character. Its projective monodromy is not unitarizable.
head: environment

label: cor:uniform-count
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply the standard uniform bound for the number of connected components of fibers of a definable set in an o-minimal structure \cite[Section~4.4]{vdDM96}. In our setting, the structure is $\mathbb R_{\mathrm{an}}$, generated by real-analytic functions restricted to compact boxes on whose neighborhoods they are analytic \cite[Section~2]{vdDM96}.

The unitary representation space is semialgebraic in the real and imaginary parts of a finite set of generator matrices: the unitary equations, determinant equations, and finitely many group relations are polynomial equations. The finite trace functions are also polynomial in these entries. By the projection theorem for semialgebraic sets, their compact image $K^{\mathrm{tr}}$ is semialgebraic.

For a closed real coordinate box $B_0$ contained in a slightly larger parameter chart, relative properness of the finite-trace map makes
\[
 \{(b,Q):b\in B_0,\ F_{X_b}(Q)\in K^{\mathrm{tr}}\}
\]
compact. Consequently, in the affine trivialization, the coefficient vectors belong to a fixed compact box. The jointly holomorphic finite-trace functions are real analytic on a neighborhood of the resulting product box. It follows that the condition of belonging to $K^{\mathrm{tr}}$ defines an $\mathbb R_{\mathrm{an}}$-definable set there. Its fiber at each $b$ is finite by the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:holonomy}. Because these fibers are finite, the bound on the number of components also bounds their cardinalities uniformly. Finitely many such boxes cover $K$. Taking the maximum of these bounds gives a uniform bound for every finite-trace preimage and hence for every $\operatorname{Hol}_{X_b}^{-1}(\mathcal K)$. The last assertion follows from the lift used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:unitary}.

label: def:spherical
title: Definition
head: environment
name: Spherical conical metrics

label: prop:metric-classes
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:metric-classes}
The quotient $\operatorname{Sph}(X,D,\boldsymbol\beta)/{\sim}$ is finite. Each class is homeomorphic to a point, to $\mathbb R_{>0}$, or to $\mathbb H^3$, according as its projective monodromy is noncoaxial, nontrivial coaxial, or trivial. In particular, all noncoaxial metrics with the fixed data form a finite set. Every continuous family parametrized by a connected space has constant Schwarzian and lies in one of these classes.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The correspondence with developing maps associates to each metric a projective connection $Q_h=\tfrac12\mathcal S(f)$ with unitarizable projective monodromy \cite[Section~2]{CWW+15}\cite[Sections~2 and~4]{Ere24}. In a local conformal expression $h=e^{2u}|dz|^2$, its coefficient is $u_{zz}-u_z^2$, with coefficient $(1-\beta_i^2)/4$ of the $z^{-2}$ term at $a_i$. Away from $D$, local univalence makes the Schwarzian holomorphic, including at poles of an affine target coordinate. The standard correspondence also gives the required local regularity at each cone and the corresponding regular-singular expansion.

Conversely, take a connection with the prescribed coefficients and unitarizable projective monodromy. Choose a solution ratio $f$ whose monodromy is in $\operatorname{PSU}(2)$. The nonzero Wronskian ensures local univalence outside $D$. At a nonintegral difference $\beta_i>0$, Frobenius theory gives $f=z^{\beta_i}a(z)$, where $a$ is holomorphic and $a(0)\ne0$, after a round rotation sending the local fixed axis to $0,\infty$. If necessary, we interchange the two axis points to obtain the positive exponent. At a positive integral difference $\beta_i=k$, a nonzero logarithmic term would produce nontrivial parabolic projective monodromy. Unitary monodromy excludes this term, so the ratio extends meromorphically with local degree $k$. The pullback of the round metric then has precisely the form \eqref{eq:cone-metric}. For $k=1$ the metric extends smoothly and positively. These are the local models used in \cite{CWW+15,Ere20c,Ere24}.

Two developing maps have the same Schwarzian if and only if they differ by a constant M\"obius transformation. Indeed, the local bases of solutions of $y''+Q_z y=0$ differ by a constant invertible matrix, and the same transformation between their ratios extends to the universal cover by analytic continuation. Hence the projective classes are in bijection with the set in Theorem~\ref{thm:unitary}, and the quotient is finite.

Fix one class and a developing map $f$ with scalar unitary lift $\rho$ on $X\setminus D$. Write every other developing map with this Schwarzian as $M\circ f$ and choose a determinant-one representative of $M$. The corresponding positive Hermitian form $H=M^*M$ defines a single-valued metric precisely when
\begin{equation}\label{eq:invariant-forms}
 H=H^*>0,\quad \det H=1,\quad
 \rho(\eta)^*H\rho(\eta)=H\quad(\eta\in\Gamma).
\end{equation}
Conversely such a form is realized by $M=H^{1/2}$. With $\mathbf v_f=(f,1)^{\mathsf t}$, its metric is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hermitian-metric}
 h_H=\frac{4|f'|^2}{(\mathbf v_f^*H\mathbf v_f)^2}|dz|^2.
\end{equation}
These metrics all have the same local angles. Distinct forms determine distinct metrics: equality in \eqref{eq:hermitian-metric} implies equality of positive Hermitian quadratic polynomials on the open image of a univalent chart, hence equality of their coefficients.

Since $\rho$ is unitary, invariance in \eqref{eq:invariant-forms} means that $H$ commutes with all its matrices. Noncoaxial projective monodromy is equivalent to the absence of a common invariant complex line for this unitary lift. A nonscalar $H$ would have invariant eigenspaces; hence $H=I$ in this case. For nontrivial coaxial monodromy, an axis basis diagonalizes the representation and some matrix has distinct eigenvalues. The invariant forms are precisely $\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})$, $t>0$. For trivial projective monodromy, all scalar matrices are $\pm I$, so every positive determinant-one Hermitian form occurs. The space of these forms is the usual model of $\mathbb H^3$.

The parametrizations are homeomorphisms. The forward map is smooth on compact subsets outside $D$. For the inverse map, we choose four regular points whose developing values give independent evaluations on the real four-dimensional space of Hermitian quadratic forms. Such points exist because a Hermitian polynomial vanishing on an open set is zero. We recover these evaluations from the metric by taking positive square roots in \eqref{eq:hermitian-metric}, and then recover $H$ continuously by solving an invertible real linear system. Finally $h\mapsto Q_h=u_{zz}-u_z^2$ is continuous in the stated topology. Since its image is a finite subset of the accessory space, $Q_h$ is constant along any connected continuous family.
head: environment

label: prop:coaxial-obstruction
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We normalize the developing map so that monodromy acts by rotations about $0,\infty$. Then $\omega=df/f$ descends to a nonzero meromorphic one-form on $X$. At a nonintegral cone it has a simple pole with residue $\pm\beta_i$. At an integral cone it has a simple pole with residue $\pm\beta_i$ if the developing value is an axis point, and otherwise it has a zero of order $\beta_i-1$. For an ordinary marked point, this order is zero. At an unmarked smooth point, zeros and poles of $f$ give simple poles of $\omega$ with residues $\pm1$. By local univalence outside $D$, there are no other zeros or poles.

Let $I$ be the complement of $J$, let $A\subset I$ be the integer marks giving poles, and let $k$ be the number of unmarked poles. The divisor degree $\deg\operatorname{div}(\omega)=2g-2$ gives
\[
 \sum_{i\in I\setminus A}(\beta_i-1)=|J|+|A|+k+2g-2,
 \quad B_g=k+\sum_{i\in A}\beta_i.
\]
The residue theorem gives signs $\eta_j\in\{1,-1\}$ such that
\[
 S_\varepsilon=-\sum_{i\in A}\varepsilon_i\beta_i-\sum_{j=1}^k\eta_j.
\]
The right-hand side is an integer whose absolute value is at most $B_g$ and whose parity agrees with that of $B_g$. This proves \eqref{eq:coaxial-signs}. If no choice of signs satisfies these conditions, every metric is noncoaxial, and the final assertion follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:metric-classes}.
head: environment

label: cor:nonintegral-metrics
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:nonintegral-metrics}
If every $\beta_i$ is positive and nonintegral and $2g-2+n>0$, then $\operatorname{Sph}(X,D,\boldsymbol\beta)$ is finite.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Here $B_g=2-2g-n<0$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:coaxial-obstruction} excludes every coaxial metric. The conclusion now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:metric-classes}.
head: environment

label: rem:coaxial-angles
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:coaxial-angles}
At $g=0$, \eqref{eq:coaxial-bound}--\eqref{eq:coaxial-signs} recover the original signed-sum and parity exclusions. The developing maps
\[
 f_t(z)=t[z(z-1)]^{1/3},\quad t>0,
\]
give distinct metrics with fixed angle parameters $(1/3,1/3,2,2/3)$ at $(0,1,1/2,\infty)$. Their monodromy consists of rotations by cube roots of unity. They have the same Schwarzian, but their leading metric coefficient at $0$ is $4t^2/9$. This example shows that three nonintegral angles can coexist with a coaxial family when an integral angle is present.

Ignoring ordinary marked points, a smooth sphere has one projective class with metric space $\mathbb H^3$, whereas a sphere with one genuine conical point admits no such metric. For two genuine points, choose coordinates $0,\infty$. The angle parameters must agree, say with value $\beta$, and $Q=(1-\beta^2)/(4z^2)$. The map $z^\beta$ gives the class; it is a positive real ray for nonintegral $\beta$, and $\mathbb H^3$ for integral $\beta\ge2$. More generally, on the sphere one nonintegral angle with all others integral is impossible, while two nonintegral angles force coaxial monodromy: after the integral peripheral monodromies become identity, the remaining two are inverse unitary rotations. On positive-genus curves, all-ordinary marked data give the empty set by Gauss--Bonnet. For the sphere with at least three genuine points and all $0<\beta_i<1$, the stronger uniqueness assertion is already known, see \cite{LT92} and \cite[Theorem~1.9 (ii)]{BGJ+19}.
head: environment
name: Sphere cases

label: cor:odd-divisors
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:odd-divisors}
Suppose $g=g(X)\ge1$ and $R$ has odd degree $d>2g-2$. Then
\[
 0<\#\operatorname{Sph}(X,R)<\infty.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
All angle parameters are integral. A coaxial metric would have $J=\varnothing$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:coaxial-obstruction}, so $S_\varepsilon=0$ and $B_g=2-2g+d$ would be even. Since $d$ is odd, this is impossible. Thus every metric is noncoaxial, and finiteness follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:metric-classes}.

To prove nonemptiness, we apply existing results on the existence of curvature-one metrics with the curve and every point of $R$ fixed. Put $a=2-2g+d$, a positive odd integer. If $a=1$, Troyanov's Theorem~C \cite{Tro91} applies: its area quantity is $2\pi a=2\pi$, which is strictly less than both $4\pi$ and twice the smallest cone angle $2\pi(m_i+1)\ge4\pi$. If $a\ge3$, the supercritical existence theorem of Bartolucci--De Marchis--Malchiodi applies \cite[Theorem~1.1]{BDM+11}; see also its original author formulation in \cite[Theorems~0.5 and~0.7]{DM10}. In its notation the singularity orders are $m_i>0$, the prescribed curvature is $1$, and the parameter is $\rho=4\pi a>8\pi$. Its exceptional set is
\[
 \left\{8\pi k+8\pi\sum_i n_i(1+m_i)>0:
 k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ n_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.
\]
Every member is an integral multiple of $8\pi$, whereas $a$ is odd. The nonresonance requirement of that existence theorem is satisfied. Together, these two cases establish nonemptiness.
head: environment

label: def:ramification-map
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:ramification-map}
Let
\[
 U_{12}=\mathbb P H^1(X,L_1\otimes L_2^{-1})^s
\]
be the open subset of classes of extensions $0\to L_1\to E\to L_2\to0$ with stable middle bundle. Its Hermitian--Einstein projective connection defines a noncoaxial metric, and the derivative of the corresponding section of the projective bundle $\mathbb P(E)$ of lines in $E$ is a nonzero section $\theta_E$ of $B_{12}$. The real-analytic map
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ramification-map}
 \mathscr R_{L_1,L_2}:U_{12}\longrightarrow\mathbb P H^0(X,B_{12}),
 \quad [E]\longmapsto[\theta_E]
\end{equation}
is the ramification divisor map of \cite[Theorems~2.3--2.4]{LSX21}.
head: environment
name: The ramification divisor map

label: prop:ramification-fibers
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:ramification-fibers}
Every fiber of \eqref{eq:ramification-map} is finite. For a nonzero section $\theta\in H^0(X,B_{12})$ with divisor $R$, the fiber is in bijection with the noncoaxial metrics in $\operatorname{Sph}(X,R)$. On each nonempty connected component of $U_{12}$, the differential of $\mathscr R_{L_1,L_2}$ has full real rank on an open dense subset. Its critical set has measure zero, and its image contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb P H^0(X,B_{12})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every extension in the fiber over $[\theta]$ gives a noncoaxial metric with ramification $R$. By the injectivity for fixed line bundles cited above, distinct points of this fiber correspond to distinct metrics. This set is finite by Proposition~\ref{prop:metric-classes}.

To prove the claimed bijection, we start with any noncoaxial metric with ramification $R$. By the stable-extension correspondence it is represented by $0\to L\to E\to M\to0$. Its ramification section gives
\[
 K_X\otimes L^{-1}\otimes M\simeq\mathcal O_X(R)\simeq B_{12}.
\]
We tensor the extension by $N=L_1\otimes L^{-1}$. The subline becomes $L_1$ and the quotient becomes
\[
 M\otimes N\simeq L_1\otimes K_X^{-1}\otimes B_{12}\simeq L_2.
\]
Tensoring preserves stability and the associated projective metric. After choosing identifications of the endpoint line bundles, we obtain a point of $U_{12}$. Its ramification section has divisor $R$ and hence differs from $\theta$ by a nonzero constant on the compact connected curve. This proves surjectivity onto the metric set, while injectivity for fixed line bundles gives the claimed bijection. Moreover, tensoring does not introduce any additional equivalence within $U_{12}$: an equivalence preserving its subline would require $L_1\otimes N\simeq L_1$, hence $N\simeq\mathcal O_X$, and the remaining endpoint changes only scale the extension class.

By Serre duality,
\[
 h^1(X,L_1\otimes L_2^{-1})=h^0(X,B_{12})=k+g-1,
\]
where the second equality follows from Riemann--Roch and $\deg(L_1\otimes L_2^{-1})<0$. Thus the source and target in \eqref{eq:ramification-map} have the same real dimension $e=2(k+g-2)$ whenever the source is nonempty. On each component of the source, let $r$ denote the maximal rank of the differential. If $r<e$, a point where the rank equals $r$ has a neighborhood on which the rank is constant and equal to $r$: a nonvanishing $r$-minor gives the lower bound and maximality gives the upper bound. The constant-rank theorem would then produce local fibers of positive dimension $e-r$, contradicting finiteness. We conclude that the maximal rank is $e$.

The analytic section $\bigwedge^e d\mathscr R_{L_1,L_2}$ is not identically zero on the component. Analytic continuation shows that its zero set has empty interior, and the standard zero-set theorem for real-analytic functions makes it measure zero \cite{KP02}. Consequently, the locus of full rank is open and dense. By the inverse function theorem, the image contains an open subset. If $e=0$, full rank holds everywhere and the same assertion is immediate.
head: environment

label: rem:rational-functions
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:rational-functions}
For $X=\mathbb P^1$, this is the familiar finite Wronski map for rational functions with a complete prescribed critical divisor \cite[Section~1]{EG01}\cite[Section~2.2]{Sch02}. Its degree is the Catalan number $\frac1d\binom{2d-2}{d-1}$, which bounds the number of distinct classes and gives the count for a general fiber. These sharper counts are classical. Degree-one maps give one class with no critical points. A map of degree at least two has at least two critical points; if exactly two occur, each has order $d-1$, and after sending them to $0,\infty$ the class is represented by $z^d$. Thus the cases of a sphere with few marked points agree with the projective-connection argument and the metric classification above.

name: Rational functions
